transcript.text: My Panasonic NN-ST45KWBPQ is sparking inside when I heat soup, little blue flashes on the right-hand wall and a crackling noise. I stopped it. Is it safe?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Stop using the microwave now: switch it off at the socket and unplug it, and don't run it again (not even empty) until we know why it sparked. Never take the outer casing off — parts inside can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged. No — do not use it again. Blue flashes and crackling are internal arcing, not normal behaviour, and it needs a qualified microwave engineer to check it before it is used. Because the flashes were on the right-hand wall, the most likely cause is food/grease contamination or damage to the small waveguide (mica) cover there. Foil, metal, or a dish with metallic trim can also cause this. 1. Remove the glass tray and check that no foil, twist-tie, metal utensil, or metallic-trimmed dish was inside.
2. Look at the small flat panel on the right-hand cavity wall. If it only has food splatter, wipe it gently with a soft damp cloth and let it dry fully. 3. If that panel is blackened, burnt, cracked or holed, or if the wall paint is chipped/rusted or there are burn marks, leave it unplugged and arrange repair. Do not remove the microwave casing or try to test it: dangerous stored high voltage can remain inside even when unplugged.

I've unplugged it. There was no foil or metal, just a plain plastic bowl of soup. The panel on the right wall looks cardboard-like and has a black burnt spot with greasy splatter on it. The paint is fine, no chips. I also saw a wisp of smoke from that spot once, which stopped when I turned it off.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. This points to the waveguide cover: the cardboard-like panel is normally mica, and grease on it can carbonise, then arc and smoke. It must remain out of use and needs a qualified microwave engineer to inspect it before it is used again. A burnt cover can sometimes be the only damaged item, but the engineer also needs to check the area behind it for heat or arc damage; it is not safe to run the microwave again to test it. With it unplugged, you may only look closely at the panel—do not remove the outer casing or investigate behind the panel. If it is cracked, holed, or crumbly, that further suggests the cover has failed. Even if it is only blackened, the smoke and repeated arcing mean professional inspection is still needed.

claimsRejected.claim: Less commonly, the cavity paint/coating or the high-voltage system is damaged.

Food splatter, foil or other metal item causing cavity arcing (medium)
Damaged cavity coating or an internal high-voltage fault (low)
